assertions.text: Output contains a @TableTest annotation

assertions.text: Multiple @TableTest methods are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing item operations, coupon logic, total calculation, and checkout.
assertions.evidence: Five @TableTest methods: addsItemsToCart, removesItemsFromCart, appliesCoupon, checksOutCart, calculatesCartTotal

assertions.text: Judge each @TableTest in isolation. The assertion FAILS if a row re-covers an obligation an earlier row in the SAME table already discharged (e.g. a full region x speed x weight cross-product where one row per rate band would state the same rule). Judge each table against its concern's coverage obligations — the distinct behaviours the rule must demonstrate. Where the expected output states those obligations for a concern, judge against that list and do not invent a stricter one; where it does not, derive them from the concern itself. A row that discharges an obligation no other row reaches earns its place however simple it looks, and a value set that covers several values in one row is the preferred discharge, never a failure. ROWS YOU THINK ARE MISSING ARE NEVER A FAILURE HERE — this assertion judges excess rows only, and coverage is judged by 2.19-covers-every-tier and quantifier-covered-by-rows. Judge every @TableTest method in the class; your evidence must name each method with PASS or FAIL.
assertions.evidence: addsItemsToCart PASS (3 distinct rows); removesItemsFromCart PASS (3 distinct rows); appliesCoupon PASS (4 distinct rows: activate, replace, expired, nonexistent); checksOutCart PASS (4 distinct rows: empty, sufficient, single short, multi short); calculatesCartTotal PASS (6 distinct rows: none, pct, fixed, product-present, product-absent, floor) — no row repeats an already-discharged obligation in any table.

assertions.text: Judge the class as a whole. The assertion FAILS if a whole @TableTest re-proves rules that earlier tables already established — an integration or end-to-end table whose rows re-prove established rules is the common case, and it fails however clean the other tables are. Sibling tables that each isolate one rule are NOT duplication merely because they share a baseline row: four surcharge tables that each show 'no surcharge' then 'surcharge applied' are four legitimate tables, not one duplicated four times. Collapsing several same-fixture tables into one, as concern-not-over-split requires, is likewise not a failure here. Rows you think are missing are never a failure here. Your evidence must name the re-proving table and the table it duplicates.
assertions.evidence: No integration/end-to-end table exists; checksOutCart only tests stock, calculatesCartTotal only tests price math, appliesCoupon only tests validity — none re-proves another table's rule.

assertions.text: Scenario names name the variation the row exercises, not the result it produces. The decidable test: FAILS when a scenario name states or paraphrases a value that appears in an expectation column of that same row — 'User cannot delete' beside an Allowed? cell of false, 'No discount applies' beside a Discount? cell of 0.00, 'Contractor gets no bonus' beside a Bonus? cell of 0. Also FAILS on generic labels ('Test 1', 'Test case 2'), which name no variation at all. PASSES otherwise. Naming the rule or the situation is correct even when it makes the outcome inferable — 'Delivery and pickup items always split', 'At the standard threshold, not above it', 'EU express, light package', 'Renewal with no claims', 'Missing name' all PASS. The failure this catches is a name echoing its own expectation cell, not a name that describes what the row is about, and not a name from which a reader who knows the rule could predict the outcome. A single offending name fails the assertion. Judge every @TableTest method in the class.
assertions.evidence: 'Unknown product is rejected' beside Success?=false and 'Discount larger than total floors at zero' beside Total?=0.00 both echo their own expectation cells.

assertions.text: @Description annotations do not merely repeat information that the scenario names already convey — e.g. coupon type behaviour (what PERCENT/FIXED/PRODUCT mean) belongs in descriptive scenario names, not duplicated in the description. It PASSES when the @Description adds what scenario names cannot: naming an interpretation as a deliberate assumption (an underspecified rule resolved a particular way), stating why a choice applies, or fixed constants. Noting an assumption is legitimate even when a row also demonstrates it — that is rationale, not redundancy.
assertions.evidence: Descriptions state assumptions like 'Message format (...) is assumed' and 'Totals are compared with BigDecimal.compareTo to ignore scale differences' rather than repeating scenario names.

assertions.text: Cell values make the rule falsifiable, not merely distinguishable. Judge each @TableTest table independently; the assertion FAILS if any table meets any of these conditions: (1) its expectation column holds the same value in every row; (2) in every row, each expectation cell is a verbatim copy of a cell in an input column of the same row; (3) an implementation that ignored the input columns entirely and returned a fixed value would satisfy every row. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Do not fail a table merely because its values are simple or round — only these three conditions matter. One exemption applies to conditions (1) and (3): a table whose claim IS an invariance — that some input does not affect the outcome — correctly holds one expectation value across every row, because that constant is the rule's subject rather than evidence of a weak table. A single row varying that input over a value set (e.g. '{DHL, UPS, FEDEX} | 12.00') is the correct compact form and PASSES, provided the title or description states the invariance. Condition (2) is not exempted.
assertions.evidence: In appliesCoupon, 'Cart After?' is '[activeCoupon: SAVE10]' in all four rows, so a fixed-output implementation would satisfy that column.

assertions.text: A reader can state the rule from the table alone, without the test method body. The assertion FAILS if any of these hold for any @TableTest: (1) a value needed to predict the expectation (a threshold, rate, cutoff, multiplier, reference date) appears only in the method body or a field, and in neither a column, the @DisplayName, nor the @Description; (2) the operation applied to the inputs cannot be named from the column headers and cell values alone. Otherwise the assertion PASSES. Setup that merely constructs the objects named by the columns is not a failure. Comparison criteria applied by a helper or the assertion body are graded by assertion-criteria-declared, not here. Judge every @TableTest method in the class. Your evidence must list each method name with PASS or FAIL beside it; a verdict reported from a subset of the methods is not a verdict. A value counts as published if it appears ANYWHERE on the test class's published surface: any @DisplayName or @Description on any method, the class-level @Description, or a column of any table. A method with no @DisplayName publishes its own name as its title, with camelCase split into words, so method names count as published text. Clause (1) triggers only when the value appears ONLY in the method body or a field — a value stated in a sibling method's @Description is published, not hidden.
assertions.evidence: checksOutCart's @Description states: 'The insufficient-stock message lists every short product as '<name>: need <required>, have <available>', joined with '; '.'

assertions.text: Each @DisplayName (or the method name it falls back to) states what the code under test does, not an external fact it depends on. Apply the check mechanically: strike the system under test from the sentence — if it still reads as true, because it merely restates a regulation, standard, format, or domain fact, the title is about something else and fails. Judge ONLY the title — the @DisplayName, or the method name it falls back to. The @Description and the scenario names are other assertions' subject; a description that restates a domain rule is not this assertion's failure and must not be cited as one.
assertions.evidence: @DisplayName('Calculates the cart total after coupon discounts') and others describe what the code does, not external facts.

assertions.text: When a title or description quantifies over a domain — 'regardless of X', 'any X', 'whatever the X', 'with or without X' — the rows must actually cover that domain. A value set discharges the promise and is the preferred way to do so: one row holding {A, B, C} both covers the domain and states the independence. Additional near-identical rows are NOT required and are NOT credited. FAILS when a quantifying claim appears and the tables show only one value of the quantified domain, or fewer values than the claim needs (e.g. 'regardless of category' with a single category anywhere in the table). PASSES when the quantified values appear, whether as a value set in one row or as separate rows; also passes when no quantifying claim is made. This assertion is about the claim matching the rows, NOT about row count. Satisfying it by adding rows where a value set would do is not an improvement and must not be scored as one, and it never requires cross-multiplying two quantified domains.
assertions.evidence: Description says discount applies 'regardless of quantity' but both product-coupon rows use Cart [Widget: 2] — no varied quantity value is tested.

assertions.text: A comparison criterion applied by the assertion must be stated on the published surface — the table, the @DisplayName, or the @Description. FAILS when a helper or the assertion body applies ordering (sorting either side before comparing), a numeric tolerance, subset or 'contains' matching, or normalisation of the actual or expected value, and no column, title or description says so. Such a criterion is a rule the test enforces and no table claims: a reader cannot tell whether order is part of the behaviour or an artefact of the comparison. PASSES when each such criterion is named — a description sentence ('the expected column lists substrings the message must contain', 'shipments are compared without regard to order') or a column that makes it evident — and passes when the assertion is a plain equality on the values the columns name. Constructing the objects the columns name is not a criterion. The title is the @DisplayName, or the method name it falls back to, with camelCase split into words. A conventional floating-point epsilon (an assertEquals delta of the order of 0.001 on a decimal column, or BigDecimal.compareTo) is numeric hygiene, not a rule, and is exempt. What this assertion is for is a criterion that changes which behaviours the test would accept — ordering, subset matching, normalisation — since those are rules the test enforces while no table claims them.
assertions.evidence: All assertions are plain assertEquals on named fields; only compareTo tolerance is used and it's declared: 'Totals are compared with BigDecimal.compareTo to ignore scale differences.'

assertions.text: Across the @TableTest methods in one class, the same observable quantity carries the same column name. FAILS when one output quantity appears under two or more names in sibling tables (e.g. 'Base Rate?' in one table, 'Rate?' in a second and 'Total Cost?' in a third for the same computed cost; or 'Cart Items' in one table and 'Cart Before' in another for the same input). A genuinely different quantity may of course have a different name — a base rate before surcharges and a final total are two quantities, and naming them differently is correct, provided the same quantity is named the same wherever it recurs. PASSES when each recurring quantity has one name throughout, and passes trivially for a class with a single table. This assertion is about naming only: it never asks for more tables or more rows, and collapsing tables satisfies it rather than violating it.
assertions.evidence: 'Cart Before'/'Cart After?' used consistently in addsItemsToCart, removesItemsFromCart, appliesCoupon; 'Catalogue', 'Success?', 'Message?' consistent across tables.

assertions.text: Do not fragment a single concern across multiple @TableTest methods that share the same fixture and assertion and differ only in which one sub-rule they exercise. Two or more tables that fix the same setup (e.g. same zone and base cost) and each vary a single option or surcharge, with the same output column, should instead be one table with a column for the varying input. FAILS when two or more such same-fixture, single-sub-rule tables exist for one concern (e.g. a separate table per surcharge). PASSES when each @TableTest addresses a genuinely distinct concern with its own inputs. This is the complement of concerns-decomposed: that forbids cramming unrelated concerns into one table; this forbids scattering one concern across many. Apply two guards when judging whether tables should be collapsed. Collapsing is right when the combined table's total row count stays small — a handful, never a cross-product — and each row still makes clear which sub-rule it demonstrates, normally through its scenario name and the varying column. Where collapsing would multiply into a cross-product, or would leave rows whose purpose is no longer legible, the tables are genuinely distinct and separate methods PASS.
assertions.evidence: Five @TableTest methods (addsItemsToCart, removesItemsFromCart, appliesCoupon, checksOutCart, calculatesCartTotal), each a distinct concern with multiple sub-rules combined into one table, not fragmented per sub-rule.

assertions.text: Read the class's test titles (each @DisplayName, or the method name it falls back to) as the sorted index a reader would scan, stripped of their tables. FAILS when the titles do not function as a catalogue: when three or more share a leading word that carries no information ('should…', 'test…', 'verify…'), so the varying subject arrives last and the list cannot be scanned; or when no single grammatical shape accounts for a majority of the titles, so no scanning pattern exists. PASSES when the varying subject comes first or early and one consistent shape runs across the family. A single title that differs from an otherwise consistent family is NOT a failure: negative and invariant claims ('carrier does not affect cost') often read best subject-first, and one such outlier does not make an index unscannable. Judge whether a reader scanning the list would find a pattern, not whether every entry matches it. Judge the set, never a title in isolation — a title that reads perfectly on its own page can still be an unscannable entry in the index, which is the failure this assertion exists to catch. A class with fewer than three @TableTest methods PASSES.
assertions.evidence: "Adds items to the cart...", "Removes items from the cart", "Applies a coupon...", "Checks out the cart...", "Calculates the cart total..." all follow a consistent verb-first shape with no filler leading words.
